extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning rigorous calculus and proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Formal epsilon–delta definitions, limit laws, continuity, differentiability, and basic sequence/series convergence results used to prove and manipulate limits and related calculus statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity function rule (Theorem 13.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If c ∈ R, then lim_{x→c} x = c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses ε–δ definition: given ε>0 take δ=ε so 0<|x−c|<δ implies |x−c|<ε. Simple, canonical example of applying the limit definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constant multiple rule (Theorem 13.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If lim_{x→c} f(x) exists and a ∈ R, then lim_{x→c} a f(x) = a lim_{x→c} f(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle a=0 as a trivial special case. For a≠0, given ε>0 choose δ from the hypothesis for ε/|a| so that |f(x)−L|<ε/|a| implies |a f(x)−aL| = |a|·|f(x)−L| < ε. Standard ε–δ scaling argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum rule (Theorem 13.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If both lim_{x→c} f(x) and lim_{x→c} g(x) exist, then lim_{x→c} (f(x)+g(x)) = lim_{x→c} f(x) + lim_{x→c} g(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given ε>0 split it (e.g. ε/2). Use the δ’s for f and g corresponding to ε/2, then take δ = min(δ_f,δ_g). The triangle inequality and |x−y|≤|x|+|y| yield the bound. Typical proof technique: epsilon-halving and min-of-deltas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference rule (Theorem 13.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If both lim_{x→c} f(x) and lim_{x→c} g(x) exist, then lim_{x→c} (f(x)−g(x)) = lim_{x→c} f(x) − lim_{x→c} g(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows directly from the sum rule and the constant multiple rule by writing f−g = f + (−1)·g.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication rule (Theorem 13.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If both lim_{x→c} f(x) = L and lim_{x→c} g(x) = M exist, then lim_{x→c} f(x)g(x) = L M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof requires extra care because g(x) may vary; use algebra to write f(x)g(x)−LM = [f(x)−L]g(x) + L[g(x)−M], then bound |g(x)| by choosing δ that makes |g(x)−M|<1 so |g(x)|<1+|M|. Split ε appropriately (e.g. ε/2 factors) and take minimum of δ’s. Standard technique: control one factor by neighborhood choice to prevent growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division rule (Theorem 13.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If both lim_{x→c} f(x) = L and lim_{x→c} g(x) = M exist and M ≠ 0, then lim_{x→c} f(x)/g(x) = L/M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof handles denominators carefully: ensure g(x) stays bounded away from 0 by choosing δ so |g(x)−M|<|M|/2, giving |g(x)|>|M|/2 and hence a bound on 1/|g(x)|. Then express f/g − L/M algebraically and control each term with suitably chosen δ’s; consider subcases for L=0 vs L≠0 in the structured proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition rule (Theorem 13.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If lim_{x→c} g(x) = L and f is continuous at x = L, then lim_{x→c} f(g(x)) = f(L).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chain δ–ε arguments: continuity of f at L gives for given ε>0 a δ' such that |y−L|<δ' ⇒ |f(y)−f(L)|<ε; then use limit of g to find δ such that 0<|x−c|<δ ⇒ |g(x)−L|<δ'. Thus f∘g tends to f(L). Highlights necessity of continuity of outer function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of continuity at a point (Definition 13.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f is continuous at x=c if lim_{x→c} f(x) = f(c). Equivalently, all three hold: (1) f(c) is defined, (2) lim_{x→c} f(x) exists, (3) lim_{x→c} f(x) = f(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any of these three conditions fail, f is discontinuous at c. Graphical illustrations and examples of which conditions fail are provided. Continuity is used to justify composition rule and many theorems in calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiability implies continuity (Theorem 13.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is differentiable at c, then f is continuous at c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof writes f(x) = [(f(x)−f(c))/(x−c)](x−c) + f(c) and takes limits: derivative gives limit of the quotient and multiply by limit of (x−c) which is 0, yielding f(c). Standard result used to relate differentiability and continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits at infinity (Definition 13.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: lim_{x→∞} f(x) = L means: for every ε>0 there exists N>0 such that x>N implies |f(x)−L|<ε. Analogously lim_{x→−∞} f(x)=L means ∃N<0 such that x<N ⇒ |f(x)−L|<ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines horizontal asymptotes and one-sided behavior at infinity. Also defines limits equal to ±∞ as divergence to infinity: e.g., lim_{x→∞} f(x) = ∞ means for any real number L there exists N such that x>N ⇒ f(x)>L. Examples include sin(x)/x → 0 as x→±∞ and x^2 → ∞ as x→∞ (diverges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence convergence (Definition 13.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence (a_n) converges to L if for any ε>0 there is an integer N such that n>N implies |a_n − L|<ε. Notation: lim_{n→∞} a_n = L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: terms get arbitrarily close to L for large n. Illustrated with examples (e.g., 1−1/n → 1). The definition parallels limits at infinity but with integer index and is the basis for analyzing convergence of series (via partial sums).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence to infinity for sequences (Definition 13.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence (a_n) diverges to ∞ if for any L>0 there exists N such that n>N implies a_n > L. Similarly for divergence to −∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalizes sequences that grow without bound. Exercise asks to show that divergence to ∞ implies divergence (i.e., no finite limit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Series convergence via partial sums (Definition 13.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: An infinite series Σ_{k=1}^∞ a_k converges to S if the sequence of partial sums s_n = Σ_{k=1}^n a_k converges to S. If the sequence of partial sums does not converge to a finite number, the series diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial sums are the core object; convergence of series is defined by convergence of s_n. Example: the geometric series Σ 1/2^k has s_n = 1 − 1/2^n → 1. Many practical convergence tests (comparison, ratio, root, alternating series) are usually used instead of direct ε–N proofs, but the tests are ultimately justified from this definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a series converges then its terms go to zero (Theorem 13.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Σ_{k=1}^∞ a_k converges (to S), then the sequence (a_n) converges to 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses partial sums: a_n = s_n − s_{n−1} and convergence of s_n implies s_n−s_{n−1} → 0. This yields the divergence test corollary: if a_n does not tend to 0 (or tends to a nonzero number), then Σ a_k diverges. Examples illustrate the test and its limitation (a_n → 0 is necessary but not sufficient for convergence; harmonic series shows divergence despite terms→0).
